issues.quote: All in one shot: one DELETE holds its locks for as long as it runs. / Requests queue behind it, and the ones that wait too long give up.
issues.problem: The clip shows the one-shot delete's locks making user requests time out (seven 'give up'), so it presents lock contention as an availability failure. The class said the opposite about locks: a hard-delete job causes no downtime, and the interviewer's locking worry is about strong consistency, not availability. The margin note right below the clip on the page (s5a:160) repeats that. What the class did say is that a one-shot delete of 100,000 rows hurts the main service's performance, so you stagger it to 'minimize the impact'. The lock and timeout model comes from the fact-check nuance for L-0284, which was left as taught and not shown on the page.
issues.evidence: L-0282, L-0284 / transcript 02:30:54 'There would not be any downtime in your service when you're ... doing hard deletes', 02:31:28 'That's not going down. That's just about being strongly consistent.'; L-0283 / 02:37:39 'Do staggered deletions to reduce the impact.' / factcheck_applied.md §3 L-0284 (left as taught)
issues.fix: Captions B1–B2: 'All in one shot: one huge DELETE puts its whole load on the database at once.' / 'Requests slow down behind it while it runs.' Show slowed requests instead of requests that give up, or add a caption label: 'Request rate and wait times are illustrative.' In the alt text, replace 'the ones that wait too long give up, seven of them' with 'requests slow down while it runs'. Keep 'Stagger it instead: 10,000 an hour, like garbage collection.'
